result:
Solution 1 is the most likely correct one, though I did not verify it rigorously.

**Dimension.** The expected collision local time is ∫₀ᵗ∫ p¹ₛ(x₀,y)p²ₛ(x₀,y)μ(dy)ds ≍ ∫₀ᵗ s^{-d/v} ds, so L(t) ≍ t^β with β = 1 − d/v. Covering-count heuristics give P(hit B(x,r)) ≍ r^{d−u+ud/v}, so the dimension is a = u(1 − d/v). The hypothesis 1 < d/u + d/v is exactly the condition a < d, which supports this value. Solution 2 gives a = u − d, which agrees only when u = v, so it is wrong. Solutions 1 and 3 agree on a.

**Logarithmic factors.** Near a collision point, the collision mass in B(x,r) is governed by the local time over time-scale r^u, so ν(B(x,r)) ≍ r^a·Z with P(Z > λ) ≍ exp(−cλ^{1/(1−β)}). The contributions from larger time-scales decay like (s/r^u)^{1−d/v−d/u} with exponent below −1, so no extra logarithm comes from them. Applying Borel–Cantelli over dyadic scales (about log(1/r) of them) gives λ(r) ≍ (log log(1/r))^{1−β}. This is the Taylor–Wendel exponent for stable regenerative sets, transported through t = r^u. So b = 0 and c = 1 − β = d/v. Solution 3's b = d/u + d/v − 1 would need a logarithm in the hitting or mass computation, and I could not find one.

This matches Solution 1, which gives (u(1 − d/v), 0, d/v). The argument is heuristic, and I did not check it against the source literature.

CHOICE: 1
